'''Eric Rodger Pianka''' (January 23, 1939  – September 12, 2022)<ref>[https://www.crofts-crowfuneralhome.com/obituary/eric-pianka Eric Rodger Pianka]</ref> was an American [[herpetology|herpetologist]] and evolutionary ecologist.<ref>{{cite news
 |title        = Eric Pianka
 |url          = http://www.biosci.utexas.edu/IB/faculty/PIANKA.HTM
 |publisher    = Biology Department at [[University of Texas at Austin]]
 |year         = 2009
 |access-date  = 2009-07-15
 |archive-date = October 11, 2014
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20141011005340/http://www.biosci.utexas.edu/IB/faculty/pianka.htm
 |url-status   = dead
}}</ref>
{{TOC limit|2}}

==Early life==
Pianka was born in [[Siskiyou County, California|Siskiyou County]] in 1939. At age 13, he was seriously injured in a [[bazooka]] blast in the front yard of his childhood home in [[Yreka, California]].<ref name="bazooka">{{cite web
 | title        = Bazooka Injuries: Personal Injuries Sustained in 1952
 | url          = http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/bazooka.html
 | date         = 
 | url-status   = dead
 | archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20140602143301/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/bazooka.html
 | archive-date = 2014-06-02
}}</ref> His left leg became [[gangrene|gangrenous]], and he lost 10&nbsp;cm of his [[tibia]], as well as the terminal digit of the middle finger on his right hand. Pianka's childhood injury left him with a short and partially paralyzed leg. In later life, his short leg resulted in spinal [[scoliosis]] and [[cervical spondylosis]].<ref name = "bazooka"/>

Pianka graduated from [[Carleton College]] (B.A., 1960) and earned his Ph.D. from the [[University of Washington]] in 1965. He went on to do postdoctoral work with ecologist [[Robert H. MacArthur]] at [[Princeton University]]. This period, during which he worked closely with the temporarily studentless MacArthur, had a major influence on Pianka's thinking.<ref>Pianka and Vitt, 2003.</ref> In 1966, with MacArthur, Pianka coauthored the paper, "On optimal use of a patchy environment".<ref>MacArthur and Pianka, 1966.</ref> Pianka frequently mentioned MacArthur in his lectures and kept a webpage for his deceased mentor and colleague.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert MacArthur website |url=http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/MacArthur.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160719045451/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/MacArthur.html |archive-date=July 19, 2016 |access-date=July 16, 2006 }}</ref> In some ways, Pianka's own research program expands upon and continues the work that he and MacArthur began.

==Career==
Since 1968, Pianka had been on the faculty of the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. His research centered on empirical and theoretical components of natural history, systematics, community and landscape ecology.<ref>{{Cite web
 | title        = Pianka lab site
 | url          = http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/
 | url-status   = dead
 | archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20060206154835/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/ 
 | archive-date = 2006-02-06
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web
 | title        = Eric Pianka's Contributions to Ecology
 | url          = http://www.bio.utexas.edu/faculty/pianka/ERP-Contributions.html
 | url-status   = live
 | archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20240603023723/http://www.bio.utexas.edu/faculty/pianka/ERP-Contributions.html
 | archive-date = 2024-06-03
}}</ref>

Pianka had performed extensive ecological investigations on vertebrate communities in three desert systems on three continents: the [[Great Basin]], [[Mojave Desert|Mojave]], and [[Sonora Desert]]s in North America; the [[Kalahari]] in Africa; and the [[Great Victoria Desert]] in [[Western Australia]]. His [[monograph]]ic treatment of this work is a landmark ecological synthesis (Pianka, 1986).{{Citation needed|date=August 2010}}

Pianka's latest work focused on lizard communities in Australia. His research projects included study of the phylogeny and ecology of a number of groups of Australian lizards and an extensive study of the unique biotic landscape produced by Australian brush fires.<ref>[http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/research.html Current research] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060807233121/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/research.html |date=August 7, 2006 }}</ref> His favorite lizard was a small Australian [[goanna]], ''[[Varanus eremius]]''.<ref>[http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/Veremius.html Varanus eremius]</ref> In his research, Pianka combined traditional field biological methods with recent technological innovations in statistical analysis, phylogenetic reconstruction, and imaging of the Earth's surface in attempts to answer major questions about evolution and ecology.

Pianka had trained other scientists and twelve of his former graduate students are professors at major universities, including [[Kirk Winemiller]], a professor at Texas A&M University,<ref>[http://wfsc.tamu.edu/winemiller/lab/ Winemiller lab] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902042526/http://wfsc.tamu.edu/winemiller/lab/ |date=September 2, 2006 }}</ref> and Raymond Huey, a professor at the University of Washington.<ref>[http://faculty.washington.edu/hueyrb/ Home – Raymond B. Huey]</ref> Additionally, he taught a range of popular undergraduate courses; he received an award for excellence in teaching from UT Austin in 1999.<ref>[http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/courses.html Undergraduate courses] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060807233030/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/courses.html |date=August 7, 2006 }}</ref>

==Texas Academy of Science speech==<!-- This section is linked from [[William A. Dembski]] -->
Pianka's acceptance speech<ref name="speech transcript">{{cite news |last= Pearcey |first= Rick |title= Dr. "Doom" Pianka speaks: transcript from the speech that started it all |url= http://www.pearceyreport.com/archives/2006/04/transcript_dr_d.php |access-date= February 26, 2012 |newspaper= The Pearcey Report |date= April 4, 2006}}</ref>  for the 2006 Distinguished Texas Scientist Award from the Texas Academy of Science<ref>{{cite web |title= 109th Meeting of the Texas Academy of Science: Program and Abstracts (2006) |url= http://www.texasacademyofscience.org/2006_Annual_Meeting_Program |publisher= Texas Academy of Science |access-date= February 26, 2012 |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120304142232/http://www.texasacademyofscience.org/2006_Annual_Meeting_Program |archive-date= March 4, 2012 |df= mdy-all }}</ref> resulted in a controversy in the popular press when [[Forrest Mims]], vice-chair of the Academy's section on environmental science, claimed that Pianka had "enthusiastically advocated the elimination of 90 percent of Earth's population by airborne [[Ebola virus|Ebola]]."<ref>{{cite news |last= M. Mims III |first= Forrest |title= Meeting Doctor Doom |url=http://www.sas.org/tcs/weeklyIssues_2006/2006-04-07/feature1p/ |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20060407005601/http://www.sas.org/tcs/weeklyIssues_2006/2006-04-07/feature1p/ |archive-date=2006-04-07 |newspaper= The Citizen Scientist |date= March 31, 2006}}</ref> Mims claimed that Pianka said the Earth would not survive without drastic measures. Mims' affiliate at the [[Discovery Institute]], [[William A. Dembski|William Dembski]], then informed the [[Department of Homeland Security]] that Pianka's speech may have been intended to foment [[bioterrorism]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.uncommondescent.com/intelligent-design/eric-pianka-time-for-an-interview-with-the-department-of-homeland-security/ |title= Eric Pianka: The Department of Homeland Security needs to interview you |work= Uncommon Descent |author= William Dembski |date= April 2, 2006}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=October 2021}} This resulted in the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] interviewing Pianka in Austin.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.statesman.com/news/content/news/stories/local/04/5PIANKA.html |title=Professor's population speeches unnerve some |publisher=[[Austin American-Statesman]] |date=2006-04-05 |access-date=2009-07-15 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070705025453/http://www.statesman.com/news/content/news/stories/local/04/5PIANKA.html |archive-date=July 5, 2007 }}</ref>

Pianka has stated that Mims took his statements out of context and that he was simply describing what would happen from biological principles alone if present human population trends continue, and that he was not in any way advocating for it to happen.  The Texas Academy, which hosted the speech, released a statement asserting that "Many of Dr. Pianka's statements have been severely misconstrued and sensationalized."<ref>{{cite web | title= Texas Academy of Science statement on Pianka | work= The Panda's Thumb | url= http://www.pandasthumb.org/archives/2006/04/texas_academy_o.html | access-date= 2006-04-08 | url-status= dead | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20060410153828/http://www.pandasthumb.org/archives/2006/04/texas_academy_o.html | archive-date= April 10, 2006 | df= mdy-all }}</ref> However, Kenneth Summy,<ref>{{cite web |title= Kenneth R. Summy |url= http://portal.utpa.edu/utpa_main/daa_home/cose_home/biology_home/biology_staff/faculty_summy |publisher= Biology Department of the [[University of Texas, Pan American]]}}</ref> an Academy member who observed the speech, wrote a letter<ref name="summy letter">{{cite news |last=Pearcey |first= Rick |title= Support for Mims on Dr. "Doom" speech |url= http://www.pearceyreport.com/archives/2006/04/press_release_u.php |access-date= February 26, 2012 |newspaper= The Pearcey Report |date= April 12, 2006}}</ref>  of support for Mims' account, saying "Dr. Pianka chose to deliver an inflammatory message in his keynote address, so he should not be surprised to be the recipient of a lot of criticism from TAS membership. Forrest Mims did not misrepresent anything regarding the presentation."

Pianka appeared on [[NBC]]-affiliate [[KXAN-TV|KXAN Austin]]<ref>{{cite news|url= http://www.kxan.com/Global/story.asp?S=4720390|date= 2006-04-03|publisher= NBC|title= UT Professor Clearing The Record On Speech|access-date= December 12, 2010|archive-date= June 23, 2008|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080623195530/http://www.kxan.com/Global/story.asp?S=4720390|url-status= dead}}</ref> and on two cable talk-shows and posted a statement on his University of Texas website that said in part:<ref name="Pianka-reply">[http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/Everybody.html What nobody wants to hear, but everyone needs to know] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101205090757/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/Everybody.html |date=December 5, 2010 }} – Eric R. Pianka</ref>
{{blockquote|I have two grandchildren and I want them to inherit a stable Earth. But I fear for them. Humans have overpopulated the Earth and in the process have created an ideal nutritional substrate on which [[bacteria]] and [[virus]]es (microbes) will grow and prosper. We are behaving like bacteria growing on an agar plate,<ref>Reference provided by Pianka in his text: [http://www.zo.utexas.edu/courses/THOC/ExponentialGrowth.htm "Exponential Population Growth"], from Pianka, E. R. ''Evolutionary Ecology''; 6th edition; Addison–Wesley; 2000; last updated online on 7 July 2007</ref> flourishing until natural limits are reached or until another microbe colonizes and takes over, using them as their resource. In addition to our extremely high population density, we are social and mobile, exactly the conditions that favor growth and spread of pathogenic (disease-causing) microbes. I believe it is only a matter of time until microbes once again assert control over our population, since we are unwilling to control it ourselves. This idea has been espoused by ecologists for at least four decades and is nothing new. People just don't want to hear it.

I do not bear any ill will toward people. However, I am convinced that the world, including ''all humanity'', WOULD clearly be much better off without so many of us. Simply stopping the destruction of [[rainforest]]s would help mediate some current planetary ills, including the release of previously unknown [[pathogen]]s. The ancient Chinese curse "may you live in interesting times" comes to mind – we are living in one of the most interesting times humans have ever experienced. For example, consider the manifold effects of [[global warming]]. We need to make a transition to a sustainable world. If we don't, nature is going to do it for us in ways of her own choosing. By definition, these ways will not be ours and they won't be much fun. Think about that.}}
As a consequence of the controversy, Pianka and members of the Texas Academy of Science received death threats.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://abclocal.go.com/ktrk/story?section=state&id=4051760 |archive-url= https://archive.today/20120707010128/http://abclocal.go.com/ktrk/story?section=state&id=4051760 |url-status= dead |archive-date= 2012-07-07 |agency= Associated Press |publisher= KTRK Houston, TX (ABC) |date= 2006-04-04 |title= Professor criticized over comments about impending pandemic }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author= Myers, Paul Z |url= http://scienceblogs.com/pharyngula/2006/04/texas_academy_of_science_getti.php |title= Texas Academy of Science getting death threats over Pianka |work= [[Pharyngula (blog)]] |publisher= scienceblogs.com |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110805152116/http://scienceblogs.com/pharyngula/2006/04/texas_academy_of_science_getti.php |archive-date= August 5, 2011 |df= mdy-all |author-link= PZ Myers }}</ref>  According to Pianka, his daughters were worried about his and their safety, and his life had been "turned upside-down by '[[Right-wing politics|right-wing]] fools'."<ref name="statesman">{{cite news |url=http://www.statesman.com/news/content/news/stories/local/04/5PIANKA.html |publisher=American Statesman |date=2006-04-05 |title=Professor's population speeches unnerve some |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070705025453/http://www.statesman.com/news/content/news/stories/local/04/5PIANKA.html |archive-date=July 5, 2007 |df=mdy }}</ref>

==Awards and accolades==
Pianka was a 1978 [[Guggenheim Fellow]], a 1981 [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Fellow, and a 1990 [[Fulbright Scholar|Fulbright Senior Research Scholar]]. He had received numerous awards, and at least three species, an Australian lizard (''[[Ctenotus|Ctenotus piankai]]'')<ref>Beolens, Bo; Watkins, Michael; Grayson, Michael (2011). ''The Eponym Dictionary of Reptiles''. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. xiii + 296 pp. {{ISBN|978-1-4214-0135-5}}. ("Pianka", p. 207).</ref> and two lizard parasites, are named after him.<ref>[http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/honors.html Honors and awards] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060807232913/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/honors.html |date=August 7, 2006 }}</ref> A symposium in his honor was held by the Herpetologist's League in 2004. The American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists passed a resolution on the word "Piankafication" to describe Pianka's influence on evolutionary biology and ecology at their business meeting in 2004.<ref>[http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/Piankafication.pdf ASIH Resolution on Piankification] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902212654/http://uts.cc.utexas.edu/~varanus/Piankafication.pdf |date=September 2, 2006 }}</ref> In this resolution, they noted that he has had "vast and immeasurable influence on several fields of evolutionary ecology" and that his "years in the field have set the standard for both natural history and for ecological studies, resulting in publications that have lain the foundation for research programs..."

Pianka received the 2006 Distinguished Texas Scientist Award from the Texas Academy of Science. He and his research were featured in a [[wildlife documentary]] on monitor lizards — "Lizard Kings" — which premiered nationally on the [[Public Broadcasting Service|PBS]] ''[[Nova (American TV program)|NOVA]]'' series in October 2009.

In 2015, Pianka was awarded the Auffenberg Medal in recognition of his extensive research on monitor lizards by the Monitor Lizard Specialist Group. In the same year, he received the highest award of the [[Ecological Society of America]], the [[Eminent Ecologist Award]],<ref>{{cite web| url= http://esa.org/history/eminent-ecologist-award/|title= Eminent Ecologist Award|publisher= Ecological Society of America| access-date= 14 August 2015}}</ref> having been elected a Fellow of the [[Ecological Society of America]] in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-06-11 |title=ESA announces 2013 Fellows |url=https://esa.org/blog/2013/06/11/esa-announces-2013-fellows/ |access-date=2025-08-12 |website=Ecological Society of America}}</ref>

==Works==
Pianka had produced about 200 scientific papers, as well as the textbook, ''Evolutionary Ecology'', which has gone through seven editions and has been translated into five languages. In 2003, he also published ''Lizards: Windows to the Evolution of Diversity'', coauthored with longtime collaborator Laurie Vitt, won the Grand Prize at the Robert W. Hamilton Faculty Author Award at The University of Texas at Austin as well as the Oklahoma Book Award from the Oklahoma Center for the Book.<ref>[http://www.ucpress.edu/books/pages/9744.html#awards Awards for "Lizards-Windows to the Evolution of Diversity"]</ref>
